scale.source: Wikipedia, "Long and short scales": "Use of the short scale is found in most English-speaking and Arabic-speaking countries"; Wikipedia, "English numerals": the short scale is "always used in American English and almost always in British English". Wiktionary, "billion": "(US, modern British & Australian, short scale) a thousand million".

group_mark.source: English writes 1,000,000.5: the comma groups digits. CLDR 49 numbers, en (latn): "'symbols-numberSystem-latn': { 'decimal': '.', 'group': ','"; Wikipedia, "English numerals": "larger numbers are written for example 10 000 or 10,000 for ease of reading".

decimal_mark.source: English writes 1,000,000.5: the point marks the decimals. CLDR 49 numbers, en (latn): "'symbols-numberSystem-latn': { 'decimal': '.', 'group': ','"; Wikipedia, "Decimal separator": "In the United States, the full stop or period (.) is used as the standard decimal separator".

space_groups.source: English groups digits with a comma ("1,000,000"). CLDR 49 numbers, en (latn): "'symbols-numberSystem-latn': { 'decimal': '.', 'group': ','". Structural, no external source: a space between digit strings separates two numbers.

plural_scale_needs_count.source: Wiktionary, "million", numeral sense 2: "(colloquial, hyperbolic) An unspecified very large number". So a plural scale word with no count ("millions of people") names no number, and one with a count ("two million people") does.

scale_noun_agrees.source: An English scale word keeps the singular after a count above one: Wiktionary, "million", usage notes: "Until the early 20th century, million behaved much like an ordinary quantificational noun" ("five millions of pounds"); the modern form is "five million pounds".

joiner_tens_units.source: Wikipedia, "English numerals": "if a number is in the range 21 to 99, and the second digit is not zero, the number is typically written as two words separated by a hyphen". So tens and units take a hyphen or a space, no "and".

joiner_after_hundred.source: CLDR 49 RBNF en: %spellout-cardinal writes no "and" ("100: << hundred[ >>];", "1000: << thousand[ >>];") and %spellout-cardinal-verbose writes one before a last group below 100 ("100: << hundred[>%%and>];", "1000: << thousand[>%%and>];", "%%and: 1: ' and =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=; 100: ' =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=;"). Wikipedia, "English numerals": in American English "many students are taught [...] not to use the word and anywhere in the whole part of a number, so it is not used before the tens and ones"; "Despite this rule, some Americans use the and in reading numbers containing tens and ones as an alternative". Both forms read the same.

joiner_between_groups.source: CLDR 49 RBNF en: %spellout-cardinal writes no "and" ("100: << hundred[ >>];", "1000: << thousand[ >>];") and %spellout-cardinal-verbose writes one before a last group below 100 ("100: << hundred[>%%and>];", "1000: << thousand[>%%and>];", "%%and: 1: ' and =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=; 100: ' =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=;"). Wikipedia, "English numerals": in American English "many students are taught [...] not to use the word and anywhere in the whole part of a number, so it is not used before the tens and ones"; "Despite this rule, some Americans use the and in reading numbers containing tens and ones as an alternative". So "and" between groups is optional.

joiner_before_round_hundred.source: CLDR 49 RBNF en: %spellout-cardinal writes no "and" ("100: << hundred[ >>];", "1000: << thousand[ >>];") and %spellout-cardinal-verbose writes one before a last group below 100 ("100: << hundred[>%%and>];", "1000: << thousand[>%%and>];", "%%and: 1: ' and =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=; 100: ' =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=;"). So "and" comes only before a last group below 100 ("two thousand and one"); a round hundred after "thousand and" is no CLDR form.

joiner_before_last_group.source: CLDR 49 RBNF en: %spellout-cardinal writes no "and" ("100: << hundred[ >>];", "1000: << thousand[ >>];") and %spellout-cardinal-verbose writes one before a last group below 100 ("100: << hundred[>%%and>];", "1000: << thousand[>%%and>];", "%%and: 1: ' and =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=; 100: ' =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=;"). Wikipedia, "English numerals": in American English "many students are taught [...] not to use the word and anywhere in the whole part of a number, so it is not used before the tens and ones"; "Despite this rule, some Americans use the and in reading numbers containing tens and ones as an alternative". So a last group joins with or without "and" ("two thousand one", "two thousand and one").

comma_between_classes.source: Wikipedia, "English numerals", the table of spoken forms: "One thousand, two hundred (and) twenty-five" for 1225, "One thousand, nine hundred" for 1900, and "One thousand (and) fifty" for 1050, with no comma before a group below a hundred. CLDR 49 RBNF en %spellout-cardinal-verbose writes the same comma ("1000000: << million[>%%commas>];", "%%commas: 1: ' and =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=; 100: , =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=;"). So a comma after a scale word links the next class when that class is a hundred or more.

part_after_joiner_needs_article.source: Wikipedia, "English numerals", fractions: 1 1/2 is "one and a half" and 6 1/4 is "six and a quarter". A part word after "and" takes the article ("forty and eighth" holds no fraction).

fraction_of_scale.source: Cambridge Dictionary, "quarter", noun (fourth part): "one of four equal or almost equal parts of something"; example: "He inherited a quarter of a million pounds on his mother's death". Merriam-Webster, "quarter", noun, sense 1: "one of four equal parts into which something is divisible"; example: "a quarter of a cup of sugar". So a fraction word, "of" and a singular scale noun with its article name that part of the scale noun: "a quarter of a million" is 250000.

ten_joins_unit_ordinal.source: Wikipedia, "English numerals": "if a number is in the range 21 to 99, and the second digit is not zero, the number is typically written as two words separated by a hyphen". "ten" is below 21 and takes no unit ("ten fifth" is 10 and 5th).

ordinal_style.source: CLDR 49 RBNF en %spellout-ordinal: "20: twent[y->>|ieth];", "100: <%spellout-numbering< hundred[ >>|th];". The words before the last are cardinal, so only the last word of an ordinal is ordinal ("twenty-first", "one hundred and first").

roman_pronoun_letters.source: English "I" is the first-person pronoun, so a series noun before "I" can mark a pronoun, not a numeral: en.wiktionary.org, English "I", pronoun: "The speaker or writer, referred to as the grammatical subject, of a sentence." ("the part I like"). A series noun in title case names a series ("Part I", "World War I"): Wikipedia, "Roman numerals": "World War I and World War II".

decimal_marker.source: "point" names the decimal point ("two point five"). Wikipedia, "English numerals": a decimal is read "as a cardinal number, followed by \"point\", and then by the digits of the fractional part" ("3.1416 is \"three point one four one six\""), and 1.2 million is "one point two million". So a multiplier after the digits multiplies the decimal: "one point two hundred" is 120.

minus.source: Wiktionary, "minus", adjective: "being a negative quantity; pertaining to a deficit or reduction"; "negative": "(mathematics) of a number: less than zero". So "minus" and "negative" before a number make it negative.

minus_idioms.source: Structural, no external source: no English idiom puts "minus" before a positive number.

ordinal_article.source: Wikipedia, "English numerals": "In spoken English, ordinal numerals and partitive numerals are identical with a few exceptions. Thus 'fifth' can mean the element between fourth and sixth, or the fraction created by dividing the unit into five pieces"; Wiktionary, "hundredth": "the ordinal form of the number one hundred". Orchestrator ruling: an article before the phrase makes it an ordinal ("the one hundredth anniversary" is 100th), and otherwise it stays a fraction ("one hundredth of a second" is 0.01).

article_one.source: "a" and "an" count one only before a multiplier ("a hundred", "a dozen", "a third"); alone they are no number.

of.source: Structural, no external source: English has no "of" that multiplies a scale word.

fraction_of.source: Orchestrator ruling, knowledge/wiki/plans/number-tagger.md, Rulings: "um terço de dúzia" = 4, a fraction of a collective noun multiplies it; "one third of a dozen" = 4 reads the same in English. Priberam, "dúzia", sense 1: "Conjunto de doze."

denominator_particle.source: Structural, no external source: English has no particle like Portuguese "avos".

class_noun.source: English names no class with a singular noun after a collective: "tens of thousands" takes the plural.

half_unit.source: In English a half before a unit takes "a" ("half a pound"), so no unit noun follows "and a half" directly.

abbreviation.source: Structural, no external source: no English number word is also an abbreviation with a period.

lone_decimal_mark.source: Wikipedia, "Decimal separator": "In the United States, the full stop or period (.) is used as the standard decimal separator". Structural, no external source: a group mark stands only between digits, so a point right before the first digit marks decimals: ".5" is 0.5. The comma only groups digits, so ",5" is no decimal.

range_cue.source: Wiktionary, "between", sense 1: "In the position or interval that separates (two things), or intermediate in quantity or degree", as in "somewhere between forty and fifty dollars". The "and" joins the two limits, so it ends the first number where the words split into two numbers, the first smaller.

roman_series_noun.source: A noun that marks a place in a series makes the Roman numeral beside it an ordinal (Wikipedia, "Roman numerals": "Capital or small capital Roman numerals are widely used in Romance languages to denote centuries."; "Book volume and chapter numbers, as well as the several acts within a play."; "World War I and World War II"). Each noun, from en.wiktionary.org: English "century": "A period of one hundred consecutive years; often specifically a numbered period with conventional start and end dates, e.g., the twentieth century, which stretches from (strictly) 1901 through 2000, or (informally) 1900 through 1999. The first century AD was from 1 to 100."; English "chapter": "One of the main sections into which a published work is divided, especially a book."; English "volume": "A single book of a publication issued in multi-book format, such as an encyclopedia."; English "part": "A portion; a component."; English "act": "(countable, drama) A division of a theatrical performance."; English "scene": "(theatre, film, television, radio) A part of a dramatic work that is set in the same place or time. In the theatre, generally a number of scenes constitute an act."; English "council": "A committee that leads or governs (e.g. city council, student council)."; English "war": "(uncountable) Organized, large-scale, armed conflict between countries or between national, ethnic, or other sizeable groups, usually but not always involving active engagement of military forces.(Can we clean up(+) this sense?)"; English "dynasty": "A series of rulers or dynasts from one family.".

roman_title.source: A regnal title before a name makes the Roman numeral after the name a regnal number (Wikipedia, "Regnal number": "Regnal numbers are ordinal numbers—often written as Roman numerals—used to distinguish among persons with the same regnal name who held the same office, notably kings, queens regnant, popes"). Each title, from en.wiktionary.org: English "king": "(countable) A male monarch; a man who heads a monarchy; in an absolute monarchy, the supreme ruler of his nation."; English "queen": "A female monarch."; English "pope": "(Roman Catholicism and generally) An honorary title of the Roman Catholic bishop of Rome as father and head of his church, a sovereign of the Vatican city state."; English "emperor": "The male monarch or ruler of an empire."; English "empress": "The female monarch (ruler) of an empire.".

roman_word.source: A Roman numeral that is also a word or a common abbreviation reads only after a strong cue ("Play CD" holds no 400). Each word, from en.wiktionary.org unless another dictionary is named: English "CD": "Initialism of compact disc."; English "DC": "Initialism of District of Columbia, a federal district of the United States of America."; English "CV": "Initialism of curriculum vitae."; English "XL": "(chiefly clothing) Initialism of extra large (the manufactured size or an item of that size)."; English "mix": "(transitive) To stir together."; English "MC": "Initialism of master of ceremonies."; English "CC": "Initialism of carbon copy."; English "CM": "(India, Pakistan) Initialism of chief minister."; English "MM": "(education) Initialism of Master of Music."; English "ML": "(programming, web design) Initialism of Markup Language."; English "MD": "Abbreviation of Maryland: a state of the United States."; English "IV": "(medicine) Abbreviation of intravenous."; English "MI": "Abbreviation of Michigan: a state of the United States."; English "CL": "(US, navy) Initialism of light cruiser, a type of warship."; English "DL": "(computing) Initialism of download.".
